1. PORTFOLIO STRATEGY AND DEFINITION OF SUCCESS
It should not simply repeat the resume in prettier typography.
For a technical career portfolio, the website should perform four jobs simultaneously:
Prove that your stated skills are backed by real work.
Make it obvious what roles you are targeting and what kind of problems you solve.
Give technical reviewers enough detail to understand your decisions.
Make it easy for recruiters or hiring managers to contact you, view your resume, inspect projects, and continue to LinkedIn/GitHub.
A visitor who lands on the homepage should understand these three things almost immediately:
What you do / what roles you target.
If someone only reads the hero, sees one featured project, and clicks one CTA, they should already have a correct mental model of you.
It is not a replacement for your resume.
It is not a giant list of every assignment you have ever completed.
It is not a technology logo wall.
It is not a place to claim skills you cannot explain in an interview.
It is not an animation showcase where the content becomes difficult to find.
Helps a recruiter decide to continue.
Unrelated to your target career direction.

APPENDIX B — RECOMMENDED ORDER OF WORK
Do not spend days polishing a hero section before you know what the hero is supposed to communicate.
The content and positioning should determine the design — not the other way around.
The finished website should communicate one clear message:

Baizid Yaldram is a Data Science graduate who can build practical, end-to-end AI and data systems — from machine-learning recommendation engines and agentic analytics platforms to deployed full-stack AI applications.
The website should then prove that claim through:
Strong positioning → Three excellent projects → Technical case studies → Working demos → GitHub evidence → Professional presentation → Easy recruiter contact.
